reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A congenital anomaly in which a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the second part of the duodenum, potentially obstructing it
Has a bimodal presentation: neonates with duodenal obstruction and vomiting, and adults presenting later with pancreatitis, peptic ulceration, or obstructive symptoms
In neonates it may produce the double-bubble sign on plain radiography and is associated with Down syndrome, malrotation, and other atresias
Many adult cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on cross-sectional imaging or endoscopy
CT or MRI with MRCP demonstrates pancreatic tissue surrounding the descending duodenum and can show the annular duct
Symptomatic obstruction is treated surgically by bypass (usually duodenoduodenostomy or gastrojejunostomy) rather than by dividing the ring, which risks fistula and pancreatitis
The encircling parenchyma may be complete or incomplete, which influences the degree of obstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Annular pancreas arises from a failure of normal rotation and fusion of the ventral pancreatic bud during embryogenesis, so that pancreatic tissue comes to encircle the descending (second part of the) duodenum instead of migrating to lie posterior to it. The resulting ring of normal exocrine pancreatic tissue, which contains its own duct system draining into the main pancreatic or bile duct, can constrict the duodenal lumen. The degree of narrowing determines whether obstruction manifests in the newborn period or only later in life, and the abnormal ductal anatomy also predisposes to pancreatitis. Because it is normal pancreatic parenchyma, the ring shares in any inflammatory or neoplastic process affecting the gland.
additionalDifferentials: Pancreatic head mass causing extrinsic duodenal compression
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiography in neonates to detect the double-bubble sign
Contrast-enhanced CT to show pancreatic tissue encircling the duodenum
MRI with MRCP to define the annular duct and biliary anatomy
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study to demonstrate the level and degree of obstruction
Upper endoscopy to assess the duodenal lumen and exclude mucosal pathology
Serum amylase and lipase if pancreatitis is suspected
redFlags: Bilious vomiting in a neonate requiring urgent evaluation for obstruction and malrotation
Superimposed acute pancreatitis with systemic upset
An associated pancreatic head mass on imaging
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic incidental annular pancreas needs no treatment and has an excellent outlook; symptomatic obstruction generally resolves well after a bypass procedure, though associated congenital anomalies in neonates influence overall outcome.
pitfalls: Dividing the pancreatic ring surgically, which risks pancreatic fistula, pancreatitis, and recurrent obstruction
Overlooking coexisting duodenal atresia, malrotation, or other anomalies in affected neonates
Attributing adult symptoms solely to the anomaly without excluding peptic disease or malignancy
Missing the diagnosis when the ring is incomplete and obstruction is subtle
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Paediatric surgery texts on congenital duodenal obstruction
Radiology reviews of pancreatic developmental anomalies
management: Manage asymptomatic incidental disease with reassurance and no intervention
Relieve symptomatic duodenal obstruction by surgical bypass such as duodenoduodenostomy or gastrojejunostomy rather than dividing the ring, which risks fistula and pancreatitis
Stabilise the obstructed neonate with nasogastric decompression and fluid and electrolyte resuscitation before surgery
Treat associated pancreatitis supportively with fluids, analgesia, and rest of oral intake
Actively screen for and manage associated anomalies including Down syndrome, malrotation, and duodenal atresia
Refer to paediatric or hepatobiliary surgery and provide pancreatology follow-up
